definition: The combining of separate ideas or parts into a new, unified whole.
example: The committee's final plan was a synthesis of the strongest ideas from all four proposals.
nuance: A synthesis builds something new and coherent from many parts, while a summary just restates material in shorter form.
prompt: A student is writing a report that draws on five scientific studies about sleep.
options: Her report offered a synthesis of the five studies, showing how their findings fit together.
Her synthesis broke a single study down into its separate parts so she could examine each one alone.
Her synthesis was a two-line recap of one study's abstract.
Her synthesis was fake data she invented to make the graph look neater.
reasons: Weaving several sources into one connected picture is exactly what the word describes.
Taking one thing apart to inspect its pieces is analysis, the reverse process.
Briefly restating a single source is a summary; nothing is being brought together.
This confuses the noun with "synthetic" in the sense of artificial or fake.

practice.prompt: A chef designs a new dish that draws on two different cooking traditions.
options: The chef made a synthesis by reheating yesterday's soup exactly as it was.
The dish was a synthesis of two cuisines, pairing Korean spices with Mexican tortillas.
The chef's synthesis was to serve the spices and the tortillas on separate plates so they never touched.
The cake's synthesis came from the imitation vanilla the chef used.
reasons: Warming up one unchanged dish combines nothing and creates nothing new.
Merging flavors from two traditions into one new creation fits the word well.
Keeping the elements apart is the opposite of uniting them.
This mistakes the word for "synthetic," meaning artificial, rather than combined.
